source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters, Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity - a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect, Learning and Instruction 102142
finding: OPENED THIS SESSION (open-access copy on pedocs, CC-BY). Confirms the headline numbers with confidence intervals. Heterogeneity is very high, so the pooled mean hides large spread. The authors call the effect asymmetric: help for novices is stronger than withholding help from experts.
numbers: Novices: d=0.505, 95% CI [0.260, 0.750]. Experts: d=-0.428, 95% CI [-0.647, -0.209]. Difference of differences d=0.971, CI [0.631, 1.312]. k=88 effects per group, j=60 studies, 176 effects, 5,924 people, sample sizes 17 to 357 (median 73), 35 journals, 1992 to 2024. Heterogeneity novices Q(87)=475.2, I2=90.87%; experts Q(88)=284.5, I2=87.55%. Databases PsycINFO and ERIC only.
limits: Only PsycINFO and ERIC searched. Learners split into two groups, often by median split. Authors say dichotomising probably causes the large heterogeneity. No moderator test on the difference of differences.
agent_relevance: Treat the crossover as real on average but noisy. Expect the cost of leaving help on for a strong agent to be smaller than the cost of removing help from a weak one. When unsure, keep the help.
quote: Our results suggest that the expertise reversal effect is robust across a wide variety of contexts.

source: Chen, Kalyuga & Sweller (2017) The expertise reversal effect is a variant of the more general element interactivity effect, Educational Psychology Review 29
finding: Not opened. Springer redirects to an auth cookie page (HTTP 303), so the text is behind a paywall for this tool. Crossref gives the DOI and confirms the title only (no abstract; online 2016).
numbers: None.
limits: Still paywalled; the 2017 paper itself was not read. The 2025 meta-analysis (d19) gives the authors' own reading: the weaker effect in primary school fits low element interactivity, a post-hoc explanation that was not tested.
agent_relevance: Any proxy for interactivity (for example the number of constraints that must be held jointly in a task) is our own design, not a tested rule.

source: Scaf-GRPO: Scaffolded Group Relative Policy Optimization for Enhancing LLM Reasoning (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2510.19807)
finding: RL training where hints are given only when a problem is still unsolved (zero reward) after an initial no-hint period. Hints come in three tiers (knowledge, planning, solution), released step by step until a rollout succeeds. This is hint use gated by measured pass rate, with hints fading as the model learns. It is a training method, not inference-time prompting.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B avg over 7 benchmarks: vanilla GRPO 45.2 -> Scaf-GRPO 50.9; AIME24 30.0 -> 43.3 (+44.3% relative). Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct avg 26.1 -> 28.8 (+10.3% rel). DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B avg 50.6 -> 53.6 (+5.9% rel). Qwen2.5-7B avg 41.5 -> 44.9. Beats LUFFY (46.6 avg) by 9.2% relative.
quote: avoid providing help when a learner can succeed independently
limits: Training-time RL with hints written by DeepSeek-R1 from ground-truth solutions. Single runs in the parts read. Not an equal-token comparison with fixed help at inference time.
agent_relevance: Closest published analogue of 'fade help by pass rate': give help only where the measured pass rate is near zero, and withhold it where the model already succeeds. Gap 2 is only partly closed (training, not inference).

source: Scaf-GRPO ablations (Sec. 4.3, Table 2, Appendix G.1)
finding: Scaffolding from step 0 (no exemption period) is worse than waiting. Giving the whole hint at once is worse than releasing it in chunks. Starting at the most concrete hint is worse than starting abstract. The result is flat for exemption lengths 10% to 40% of training.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B: hints from the very beginning = -9.2% relative vs full framework. Full-hint (non-incremental) variant -6.3%. Solution-only hints 48.4 vs full 50.9 avg (-4.9%). Removing the solution tier 48.0, planning tier 48.6, knowledge tier 49.2. No chunking 47.7. Exemption 10-40%: avg 49.5 to 50.9. No guidance 45.2.
limits: One model for the ablations; the exemption length is a share of training steps (15%), tuned on the same benchmarks. Differences of 1 to 2 points on 7 benchmarks (AIME has only 30 problems) are within noise.
agent_relevance: Supports 'start without help, then help only on failure' and 'give the minimum hint first'. Always-on help is the worse arm, the same direction as expertise reversal, but this is hint dependency in training, not redundancy at inference.

source: QuestA: Expanding Reasoning Capacity in LLMs via Question Augmentation (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2507.13266)
finding: During RL, a fraction p of a reference solution is prepended to problems whose base pass rate is near zero. The hint fraction is faded: 50% for 100 steps, then 25% for 1,900 steps. The faded curriculum beats fixed 50% hints at equal 2,000 steps.
numbers: Nemotron-1.5B avg 53.14 (AIME24 61.77, AIME25 49.50). Fixed Partial-50: avg 60.26. Faded 50->25: avg 63.26 (AIME24 72.50, AIME25 62.29, HMMT 41.67). Hints only on problems with near-zero pass rate (26K filtered to at most 10K).
quote: gradually reduce reliance on hints to align the learned policy with the evaluation distribution
limits: Training-time; hint steps come from a stronger model (DeepSeek-R1). Two-stage fade, one run; no test of one-failure vs two-failure triggers.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that fading hints beats holding them fixed, and that help is targeted at items with near-zero pass rate.

source: QuestA ablations (Table 3, Table 6, Fig. 11-12)
finding: Fading further from 25% to 0% hints gave no gain. Training on the same hard problems without any hint reached a similar score but needed about twice the steps. So help sped learning and added a little; removing it fully gave no extra benefit but no visible harm either.
numbers: With hint 2K steps avg 63.26; with hint 1.1K steps avg 61.05; same data without hint 2K steps avg 60.44 (diff +2.82). Fixed Partial-50 for 2,000 steps avg 60.26. Partial-50 -> 25 -> 0 'did not yield significant improvements'.
limits: The 2.82 average difference is from single runs. Entropy fell after 100 steps at 50% hints, which motivated the switch point.
agent_relevance: Part of gap 9: fading too far gave no gain and no measurable cost; the cost lies in holding help too long. It is training, so treat it as a hint only for inference.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting (arXiv 2506.07142)
finding: On GPQA Diamond (198 questions, 25 trials each, 4,950 runs per prompt per model), a 'think step by step' scaffold raises average accuracy of non-reasoning models but raises the error rate on questions they would otherwise always get right. Many models already do CoT unprompted, so the scaffold is redundant for them.
numbers: Step-by-step vs direct, average rating: Gemini Flash 2.0 +0.135, Sonnet 3.5 +0.117, GPT-4o-mini +0.044 (p=.067). Strict 25/25 metric: Sonnet 3.5 +0.101, GPT-4o +0.01 (ns), Gemini Flash 2.0 -0.131, Gemini Pro 1.5 -0.172 (p<.001). Versus default (no suffix): Flash 2.0 +0.062, GPT-4o +0.069, Sonnet 3.5 -0.019 (ns), GPT-4o-mini +0.004 (ns).
quote: CoT can introduce more variability in answers, sometimes triggering occasional errors in questions the model would otherwise get right.
limits: One benchmark, one simple CoT prompt, temperature 0. Redundancy here means the model already does CoT by default.
agent_relevance: A clean agent-side redundancy effect: the same scaffold gains on hard items and loses on easy ones. Supports gating by item difficulty or by what the model does by default.

source: Meincke et al. (2025), reasoning-model results (o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini Flash 2.5)
finding: For models that reason internally, a CoT prompt changes accuracy only slightly and costs 20% to 80% more time. One reasoning model got significantly worse.
numbers: Average rating change from CoT vs direct: o3-mini +0.029 (p=.024), o4-mini +0.031 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -0.033 (p=.005). Flash 2.5 on the 25/25 metric -0.131 (p<.001), on the 23/25 metric -0.071 (p=.016). o4-mini on the 51% metric +0.056 (p=.003).
limits: The direct condition for Flash 2.5 may still reason internally. Single benchmark. Effects are small and mixed in sign: 'little to gain', not 'harmful'.
agent_relevance: Third-party measurement for gap 8 on explicit CoT scaffolds for reasoning models: near-zero gain, occasional loss. It is not a few-shot ablation.

source: Cheng & Mastropaolo (2026) An Empirical Study on the Effects of System Prompts in Instruction-Tuned Models for Code Generation (arXiv 2602.15228)
finding: 360 configurations (4 models, 5 system prompts of increasing detail, 3 prompting strategies, 2 languages, 2 temperatures). More detailed system prompts did not raise correctness monotonically. At T=0 the 1.5B Qwen coder model lost significantly with the Robust, Reason and Edge prompts while the larger models were flat. At T=1 the 7B and 32B models gained from richer prompts while the 1.5B lost.
numbers: Java pass@1, zero-shot, T=0: Qwen-1.5B Base 32.61; Struct 35.65; Robust 27.39; Reason 26.96; Edge 26.52 (p<0.05 vs Base for the last three, OR about 0.30-0.37). Qwen-32B Base 37.39, other prompts 35.2-37.4 (flat). GPT-20B Base 39.57, Struct 42.17, Robust 37.83.
limits: Small benchmark (percentages imply about 115 tasks per language), pass@1, 4 models. Prompt-detail levels are not matched for token count. pdftotext garbled the table layout, so figures were read from table rows and running text.
agent_relevance: Capacity-floor pattern for prompt detail: the smallest model is hurt by long constraint prompts, the large ones are flat or helped. This is the opposite model-size direction to an expertise reversal.

source: Cheng & Mastropaolo (2026), few-shot results (RQ2.1, Table 5)
finding: Fixed 3-shot examples sharply hurt the larger Qwen coder models under the base system prompt, and the loss was undone only by richer system prompts. The small 1.5B model was stable and gained mildly from structure.
numbers: Java, 3-shot fixed, Base prompt: Qwen-32B 6.96 (zero-shot Base 37.39); Qwen-7B 13.04; Qwen-1.5B 29.57 (zero-shot 32.61). Recovered to 29.57 (Qwen-32B, Robust prompt), 28.70 (Qwen-7B, Edge); Qwen-1.5B best 35.22 (Struct).
limits: Table layout garbled; the 6.96 and 13.04 figures come from running text. Such a large collapse more likely reflects output-format breakage by the examples than lost reasoning. The paper says only 'larger code-specialized models'. Not a reasoning-model result.
agent_relevance: A measured case where examples hurt larger models more than the smallest, as expertise reversal predicts, but check format interference before reading it as redundancy.

source: Levy, Ben-David Jacoby, Goldberg (2024) Same Task, More Tokens: the Impact of Input Length on the Reasoning Performance of LLMs (arXiv 2402.14848)
finding: With the same reasoning task padded to longer input, accuracy falls well before the context limit, and CoT prompting does not fix it for most models. This isolates length from content.
numbers: Average accuracy over tested models drops from 0.92 to 0.68 at 3,000 tokens of input. Lengths from 250 to 3,000 tokens.
limits: Padding is irrelevant text, not scaffold. Models are 2023-2024 generation. Says nothing about useful but redundant help.
agent_relevance: A floor for the cost of length itself: a long schema may cost accuracy even if every line is correct. Part of gap 10.

source: Li et al. (2025) Small Models Struggle to Learn from Strong Reasoners (arXiv 2502.12143)
finding: Models of about 3B parameters and below do not gain from long chain-of-thought distilled from a large teacher and do better on shorter, simpler chains. A mixed-length dataset closes much of the gap. This is a capacity limit on how much reasoning scaffold a small model can use.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct gains more than 8 points on MATH and AMC with Mix-Long over direct long-CoT training, and more than 7 points on MATH, AIME and AMC with Mix-Large over strong-teacher CoT. Students from 0.5B to 70B (Qwen2.5 and Llama families).
limits: Fine-tuning, not prompting. The gap is measured on distilled training data, not on help in the prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a small model hurt by rich help shows a learnability floor, and a pass-rate fade rule would see a low pass rate and keep help on. Track a size-dependent cap on scaffold complexity separately from the pass-rate rule.

source: Yan et al. (2025) Learning to Reason under Off-Policy Guidance, LUFFY (arXiv 2504.14945)
finding: Mixes expert reasoning traces into RL rollouts, with imitation used mainly when the model's own rollouts fail. Helps small, instruction-tuned and weak models, including cases where plain on-policy RL fails.
numbers: Over +6.4 average points across six math benchmarks vs prior RLVR, +6.2 on out-of-distribution tasks. Over on-policy RL: +8.0 on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, +3.6 on Llama-3.1-8B, +5.5 on Qwen2.5-Instruct-7B.
limits: Gating is by rollout failure, not an explicit fade schedule. No strong-model arm without help.
agent_relevance: Second independent group showing help aimed at failing rollouts works, and that weak models still benefit from help in this form.

source: Computation for this study (Wilson interval and binomial tail), script D:/research_scratch/A08.04/tmp/A08.04_noise.py
finding: Computed, not a literature source. A class pass rate measured on few tasks cannot locate a threshold. At n=10 an observed 8/10 has a 95% interval of 0.49 to 0.94. A rule 'fade when pass rate is at least 0.8' fires with probability 0.38 when the true rate is only 0.70, and 0.68 when it is exactly 0.80 (n=10).
limits: Assumes independent tasks with one shared success probability. Real classes mix easy and hard tasks, which makes the class pass rate noisier than the binomial. Not tested on a real agent.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a two-in-a-row rule cuts false fades at true 0.7 from 0.38 to 0.15 at the cost of slower fading at true 0.8. With the asymmetric cost in K02, prefer the two-batch trigger.

source: Gorbunova, Kapuza, Chen, Costley (2025) Rethinking pre-training, Frontiers in Psychology 16:1628047 (PMC12367772), power analysis and design
finding: Re-read for gap 6. Everyone received pre-training (concept maps plus glossary). Prior knowledge was split at the median into lower and higher groups, and the within-subject factor was phase (pre-training vs problem solving). No group went without pre-training, so a reversal on support cannot be tested.
numbers: N=136 university students. A priori power: assumed eta2=0.06 (f about 0.25) taken from Jung et al. 2024 (eta2 0.06 to 0.09), alpha .05, power .80, 2x2 mixed ANOVA, required n=125. Effect sizes are generalized eta squared.
limits: Power is for a medium-small effect and was just met (136 vs 125). Median split loses information. Cognitive load was self-rated.
agent_relevance: A weak test of expertise reversal. Do not count it as a failed replication in K06.

source: Rey & Buchwald (2011) JEP: Applied 17:33; Rey & Fischer (2013, online 2012) Instructional Science 41; Tobias (2009) Instructional Science 37 commentary
finding: Bibliographic records confirmed through Crossref (DOIs 10.1037/a0022243, 10.1007/s11251-012-9237-2, 10.1007/s11251-009-9103-z). Full texts are paywalled and were not opened, so their rival-explanation arguments (motivation, aptitude-treatment interaction) stay known only from earlier secondary reading.
numbers: None.
limits: Gap 7 stays open for primary text.
agent_relevance: An LLM analogue of motivation does not exist; the analogue of aptitude-treatment interaction is a capacity-by-scaffold interaction (d09, d12).

source: Working memory and instructional fit: reintroducing aptitude-treatment interaction in education research (2025, PMC12189472)
finding: Review that frames expertise reversal as one ATI case: worked examples help low-working-memory learners, and high-capacity learners can move to problem solving earlier. It cites Kalyuga 2007 and Renkl on gradual fading but reports no new effect sizes on reversal.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Narrative review; no pooled or experimental estimate separating ATI from prior knowledge.
agent_relevance: Supports the split asked for in gap 3: capacity and task familiarity predict different fixes, so measure both.

source: Kwon et al. (2025) ReasonIF: Large Reasoning Models Fail to Follow Instructions During Reasoning (arXiv 2510.15211)
finding: Reasoning models rarely follow instructions about how to reason (formatting, language, length) inside their reasoning trace, and adherence falls further as task difficulty rises.
numbers: The highest instruction-following score is below 0.25 across open models (GPT-OSS, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1), so fewer than 25% of reasoning traces comply.
limits: Measures compliance, not task accuracy. Not about scaffold length.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that tells a reasoning model how to think may be only partly obeyed, so its effect may be smaller than its length suggests.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025) meta-analysis, moderator tables 1-3
finding: Three moderators were tested: educational status, content area, and how prior knowledge was assessed. Each was significant on at least one side. Element interactivity and assistance type (worked example, hint, fading) were NOT coded as moderators. The effect looks weak in primary school and in language and humanities, strong in higher education and in law, business, crafts.
numbers: Educational status R2=25.92% (novice side), 8.47% (expert side). Novice effect by level: primary -0.29 (2 studies, reference), secondary 0.70 (CI 0.07 to 1.31, 3 studies), vocational 0.63 (4 studies), higher education 0.99 (CI 0.34 to 1.63, 22 studies), mixed groups 1.05. Content area R2=20.59% (novice side): other (law, business, crafts) 1.24 (CI 0.42 to 2.05, 6 studies) is the reference; STEM and humanities and language are lower (-0.76 and -1.08 relative to it). Content area not significant on the expert side. Prior-knowledge assessment moderated the expert side, R2=50.00%: expert effect largest when groups were defined by grade level (-0.95, CI -1.32 to -0.58) and weakest when defined by a test or intervention (coefficients +0.74 and +0.75 relative to grade level, so about -0.2 net).
limits: Table values for non-reference levels are differences from a reference level, not raw effects. Several cells have 2 to 8 studies. Moderators overlap (domain with age). Authors say the few studies per cell make inferences less reliable.
agent_relevance: The reversal is largest when the novice and expert groups are far apart (different grades or professions) and weak when one class is split by a short test. A model split by its own pass rate is the weak kind. Do not expect a large expert-side harm from a within-model split.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025), publication bias and asymmetry checks
finding: Publication bias was checked with funnel plots, trim-and-fill and Egger's regression; none was found. The check is limited because only published papers were searched; the authors suggest a community call for unpublished work. The pooled difference (0.971) is smaller than the 1.72 average in Kalyuga (2007) because of study weighting and clustering of effects.
numbers: Egger tests: novices z=0.568, p=.57; experts z=0.299, p=.77. Kalyuga (2007) narrative review: d from 0.45 to 2.99 over 26 studies, mean difference 1.72. Meta-analytic difference 0.971 (CI 0.631 to 1.312).
limits: Egger tests have low power when heterogeneity is this high. Two databases only.
agent_relevance: Use 0.5 and -0.43 as priors, not 0.86 per side. This closes the main part of gap 1 and part of gap 8: no sign of selective publication, studies spread over 35 journals.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025), discussion on adaptation and what is not known
finding: The authors say the meta-analysis cannot choose between theories (cognitive load, assistance dilemma, motivation). They say knowledge and assistance are continuous and dichotomising is the likely cause of the heterogeneity. They advise assessing knowledge repeatedly because learners gain knowledge at different rates, and point to tutoring systems with a persistent student model. When in doubt, give assistance rather than withhold it.
numbers: No new numbers. Footnote: an ordinal interaction in the observed range becomes disordinal as the range of prior knowledge grows; if linear, the crossover point can be estimated.
limits: The practical advice is a design argument. The meta-analysis tested no adaptive rule.
agent_relevance: Supports a continuous, per-item, repeatedly updated measure for fading rather than one fixed class pass-rate cut. Gap 3: the literature offers the tutor student-model idea but no tested rule for LLM loops.

source: SkillsBench v4 (arXiv 2602.12670v4), Appendix D.6 and Table 6, self-generated skills protocol
finding: Full protocol of the self-generated condition read. A creator session uses Anthropic's skill-creator and is told not to solve the task; a fresh solver session then uses the generated packs. Three configurations. All fall below the no-help baseline. Claude Code self-generated runs used effort max while its baseline used high.
numbers: Pass rates, 87 tasks, 3 trials each: Claude Code Opus 4.7 43.0 -> 34.9 (-8.1), curated 61.2 (+18.2). Codex GPT-5.5 46.8 -> 35.5 (-11.3), curated 66.5 (+19.7). Gemini CLI 3.1 Pro 36.0 -> 24.5 (-11.5), curated 60.8 (+24.8). Scored slots 258, 258 and 253 of 261. Table 6 prints the post values (the earlier note that 34.9 was derived is corrected).
limits: Effort-level mismatch on Claude Code. The creator step costs tokens, so equal-token comparison is not met. Row-to-model pairing of the Codex and Gemini values was read from garbled PDF text; the deltas are as printed.
agent_relevance: A scaffold the agent writes for itself with no verifier is a cost, not a help. Self-written parts of our schema need a check before use.

source: SkillsBench v4, Appendix D.6.1 trajectory audit of self-generated skills
finding: Audit of 12 solver trajectories over 10 task-configuration pairs gives four causes. (1) Generated packs go unused: in 10 of 12 Codex and Gemini trajectories the word skill never appears. (2) Authoring displaces solving: creator and solver share one context in Claude Code. (3) Used packs lock in confident wrong assumptions: on 3d-scan-calc a pack hard-coded a 1000x unit conversion and both trials were off by three orders of magnitude. (4) The best win was leakage: the pack was written inside the graded sandbox and named the verifier's checks.
numbers: 10 of 12 audited trajectories never mention the packs. Best case fix-visual-stability: self-generated 1.0 vs curated 0.0 on Claude Code. The 3d-scan-calc verifier was patched later, so some zeros are artefacts.
limits: Small sample chosen for extreme gaps. Creator sessions for the pre-baked family are not released. Not a controlled test of cause.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5: the harm is mostly non-use, displaced effort and confident wrong content, not length. In our schema the risky guardrails are those the agent writes for itself early (assumptions, units, conventions); generic checks tied to a verifier are safer.

source: SkillsBench v1 (arXiv 2602.12670v1), self-generated condition and Finding 3
finding: Gap 7 closed. The early version used a different method: the agent was prompted inside the same task to write 1 to 5 skill documents first, then solve. It ran on 5 of 7 configurations (Claude Code with 4 models, and Codex GPT-5.2). The later version separates creator and solver sessions and tests three newer configurations. So -8 to -11.5 pp is a different protocol, not a revision of the same measurement.
numbers: v1: self-generated -1.3 pp average; Opus 4.6 +1.4 pp; Codex GPT-5.2 -5.6 pp; curated +16.2 pp; 84 tasks, 11 domains. v4: 87 tasks, 8 domains, -8.1 to -11.5 pp on three configurations.
limits: Models, tasks, harness settings and protocol all differ between versions. No same-configuration comparison exists.
agent_relevance: Always cite the version. Self-written help ranges from about zero to -11 pp depending on protocol; the sign is stable, the size is not.

source: SkillsBench v4, Section 5, Appendix F.3, F.2 and M.8: tasks where help hurts
finding: Gap 4 partly closed. The paper names the negative-delta tasks and explains them by skill design, not by baseline strength. The text prints no per-task table of baseline against delta; per-task data appear only in heat-map figures (Figures 11 to 13). So whether negatives are the high-baseline tasks is still untested in the text. Three patterns: a heavy pipeline crowds out a simpler path; the skill displaces a stronger native strategy; the skill points to a solver the agent cannot debug.
numbers: 13 of 87 tasks negative. Largest: exam-block-sequencing -7.4, suricata-custom-exfil -7.4, adaptive-cruise-control -5.6, mars-clouds-clustering -5.6, r2r-mpc-control -5.6, econ-detrending-correlation -5.6. Top-10 beneficiaries mean +67.0 pp (llm-prefix-cache-replay 1.9% -> 94.4%). Difficulty: core 6, extended 53, extreme 28 tasks. Normalised gain g is defined; the authors say it can overstate small gains near the ceiling.
limits: With three trials per task a 5.6 pp change is one trial in 18, so many small negatives may be noise.
agent_relevance: Closer to an over-prescribed procedure than to expertise reversal. The fix is help with applicability limits and a fast path, which fits a schema that can skip steps.

source: Starace (2026) Scaffold Effects on GAIA: A Controlled Comparison (arXiv 2606.08529)
finding: Closest controlled study found for gap 2. Pre-registered, three scaffolds (ReAct, Planner-Actor-Rater, planner-then-executor), five models from three providers, GAIA Levels 1 and 2, three attempts per question, tasks fixed. Scaffold choice moves accuracy by up to 28 points within one model. The pre-registered prediction that stronger models are less scaffold-sensitive was rejected in direction at Level 2: the strongest Anthropic model gained most from structure. No case of structure hurting the strongest model was shown, but the scaffold varies architecture, not amount of help, and tokens are not matched.
numbers: Best-minus-worst scaffold gap, primary slice. Level 1: Opus 0.13, Gemini 0.06, GPT-5.5 0.04, Haiku 0.23. Level 2: Haiku 0.20, Sonnet 0.10, Opus 0.14, Gemini 0.17, GPT-5.5 0.06. Robust slice Level 2: Haiku 0.26, Sonnet 0.22, Opus 0.28 (Opus best 0.84 vs worst 0.56). Scaffold-by-model interaction chi2(8)=82.95 primary, 122.18 robust, 81.38 intersection, all p<0.0001. Level 1 robust gaps fall with tier: 0.25, 0.13, 0.03.
limits: Single author, preprint. An SDK defect suppressed some scaffold results (handled by a robust slice). Reasoning mode off. Scaffold design is not the same as amount of help.
agent_relevance: The reversal picture is not confirmed for agent structure: a strong model can gain most from structure on hard tasks. The sign depends on task level and model family. Do not assume a strong agent needs less structure; fade help per task level.

source: Mehtiyev and Assuncao (2026) Beyond Resolution Rates: Behavioral Drivers of Coding Agent Success and Failure (arXiv 2604.02547)
finding: Observational study of 9,374 trajectories from 19 agents (8 frameworks, 14 LLMs) on 500 tasks. Swapping the LLM inside one framework moves resolution far more than swapping the framework with the LLM fixed. The framework (prompt and scaffold) effect shrinks across successive Claude generations. The authors suggest lean prompts for strong models and richer prompts for weaker ones.
numbers: LLM swap: 51.5 pp across 6 LLMs in SWE-agent; 31.5 pp across 6 in OpenHands. Framework effect with LLM fixed: 3.8 pp for claude-4-sonnet and 19.4 pp for claude-3.5-sonnet; gap narrows 19.4 -> 3.8 -> 0.9 pp across three Claude generations; at the frontier 5 frameworks fall within 10 pp of the best. Agents sharing an LLM agree on 85 to 93% of tasks.
limits: Observational, not randomised. Frameworks differ in many ways at once, not only amount of help.
agent_relevance: Best match to a crossover in agents so far: scaffold gain falls as the model improves. It is a decay of benefit, not a measured harm. Supports fading in S0 but needs a controlled test.

source: Rodionov (2026) Improving Environment-Agnostic Agents: The Role of Scaffolding (arXiv 2610.22289v3)
finding: Tests a Codex-based agent on ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze and Terminal-Bench. In AGI Maze, seven tutorial levels before the target level lowered the score for both GPT-5.5 variants at both effort settings; with GPT-5.6-sol they helped at xhigh and were mixed at max. A one-line prompt change (stop and report difficulties) raised mean AGI Maze score in seven of eight comparisons. A task-specific reference agent still beat the general one, so supplied procedure still matters for these models.
numbers: Stop-and-report: higher mean AGI Maze score in 7 of 8 comparisons, differences -0.20 to +5.23 pp. A scripted reset controller recovered 34 to 60% of the gap to the ARC-AGI-3-specific agent.
limits: Few comparisons. Gains cost more tokens, and the paper says it cannot separate better information use from extra inference.
agent_relevance: A case where extra worked experience hurt a strong agent, with a sign that depended on model and effort. Test example help per model and effort setting.

source: Kaiser et al. (2025) CogniLoad: tunable length, intrinsic difficulty, distractor density (arXiv 2509.18458)
finding: Gap 6 partly closed on the measurement side. Intrinsic difficulty d is the number of interacting entities and attributes in a logic puzzle, a direct element-interactivity dial. Across 22 reasoning models, the d coefficient in a logistic fit is negative for every model, and each model gets a threshold (ID50, the interactivity at which it falls to 50%). Task length was the dominant limit; distractors gave a U-shape. No scaffold or hint condition was tested, so whether interactivity predicts scaffold benefit is untested.
numbers: 22 models; d and N coefficients significant and negative in all; gpt-5 and o3 lead with effective context length above 300 statements; four small models (DS-Qwen-7B, Phi-4-mini-reasoning, DS-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B) do not reach 50% even at mean load. Quadratic distractor term improved AIC in 18 of 22 models.
limits: Synthetic logic puzzles only. Element interactivity is defined by construction and may not match real agent tasks.
agent_relevance: A recipe: count the items that must be handled jointly, fit a per-model tolerance, give the heavy scaffold only above it. Not yet tested for scaffold benefit.

source: Search check for an R1-style 'few-shot hurts' ablation with numbers (DeepSeek-R1 report arXiv 2501.12948 and commentary)
finding: Gap 9 stays open. Web summaries repeat that few-shot prompting degrades R1, with a note that it concerns R1-Zero and detailed chain-of-thought examples. None gives the zero-shot against few-shot table. A blog toy test (RL model 85% zero-shot to 70% few-shot; supervised model 78% to 82%) is anecdotal. Firmer numbers on related effects are d07, d08, d09 and d10.
numbers: No reliable vendor numbers found.
limits: Only search results seen; the report itself was not re-opened in this step. The toy test states no sample size.
agent_relevance: Treat 'few-shot hurts reasoning models' as a model-dependent prior; test examples per model before putting any in the scaffold.

source: Kalyuga and Sweller (2004, 2005) rapid assessment of expertise and adaptive e-learning
finding: Gap 3: the human template for an adaptive trigger. A rapid test of what the learner can do correlates with a full test; the 2005 study used rapid tests plus a load rating to choose the next step in an algebra tutor, with a yoked control. The experimental group gained more knowledge and efficiency. Only search-result summaries were seen.
numbers: 2004: correlation up to .92 between rapid and traditional measures (Grades 9 to 10, algebra and coordinate geometry). 2005: experimental group higher in knowledge and cognitive efficiency than yoked control; no effect size seen.
limits: Summary-level only. Same research network as the founding studies. Uses a subjective load rating that an LLM does not have.
agent_relevance: The agent analogue of a rapid test is a short verified probe of the current item class before deciding how much help to give. Verifier outcome and token use are possible stand-ins for the load rating, untested.

source: Search check for independent failures to replicate (Nievelstein et al. 2013 legal reasoning; a 2012 computer-based partial replication; a 2009 middle-school partial effect)
finding: Gap 8 narrowed, not closed. Searches found mixed or partial outcomes outside the founding network: a worked-example effect for both novice and advanced law students with no expertise reversal in a less structured task (Nievelstein); a computer-based study that replicated reversal for transfer but not retention (2012); a middle-school study with a partial reversal on a transfer test (2009). No registered replication of Kalyuga 1998 or 2000 was found. The 2025 meta-analysis (d20) found no publication-bias signal.
numbers: Not read; no numbers taken.
limits: Snippet level only. The null in law tasks may reflect low task structure or low element interactivity, not failure of the effect.
agent_relevance: The effect depends on task structure and on the outcome measure. Test transfer-type outcomes separately from plain accuracy.
